title: Using a pipe bender on 15 mm copper pipe
subtitle: Form smooth, accurate bends in 15 mm copper pipe using a lever-type pipe bender to avoid the need for elbow fittings
excerpt: How to use a lever-type pipe bender to bend 15 mm copper pipe. Covers loading the pipe into the bender, aligning the bend mark, making the bend, and checking and adjusting the angle.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK trade plumbing practice for copper pipework installation.

glossaryTerms.definition: The curved shaped wheel around which the pipe is bent in a lever-type pipe bender. The former matches the inside radius of the bend and supports the pipe internally as the lever arm is pulled. Using the correct former for the pipe diameter prevents the pipe from kinking or flattening at the bend.

The straight roller or plate in a pipe bender that bears against the back (outer curve) of the pipe during bending, preventing the pipe wall from collapsing outward. The back guide and the former work together: the former shapes the inside of the bend and the back guide supports the outside.

content.text: A pipe bender makes smooth bends in copper pipe without kinking or flattening the bore, removing the need for a fitting where a run changes direction. The
together support the pipe wall through the bend. INTERMEDIATE: the correct loading sequence and a steady pull are consistent once practised.

Mark the pipe at the centre point of the intended bend with a pencil. The former on most lever benders has a centreline mark: this mark aligns with the pencil mark on the pipe when loading. If the bend is at the end of a measured run, account for the fact that the pipe shortens slightly on the outside of the bend: add approximately 5 mm to the nominal bend position for a 90-degree bend in 15 mm pipe.
Load the pipe into the bender

Place the pipe in the groove of the former, aligning the pencil mark with the centreline on the former. Clip the back guide over the pipe to seat it between the guide and the former. The pipe should be held firmly but not gripped so hard it cannot move along its length as the bend forms. Do not kink the pipe: ensure it is straight in both directions before applying leverage.

Hold the fixed arm of the bender steady against your thigh or against a firm surface. Pull the lever arm smoothly toward you in a continuous arc, watching the angle gauge on the former. Pull slightly past the required angle because copper springs back a small amount when released. A 90-degree bend requires pulling to approximately 95 degrees.

Remove the pipe from the bender and check the angle with a combination square or by holding it against a known true corner. To add a degree or two, reload and apply a short additional pull. To reduce the angle slightly, copper can be carefully bent back a small amount by hand over the bender former. Avoid overbending: correcting more than a few degrees introduces a flat spot.

attrs.symptom: Pipe kinks at the bend point instead of curving smoothly
attrs.cause: The back guide was not seated correctly against the pipe, leaving the back wall of the pipe unsupported during the bend.
attrs.fix: Use the bent section for a non-structural application if the bore is still round. For a new bend, ensure the back guide clips fully over the pipe before starting.

attrs.symptom: Pipe rotates in the bender rather than bending
attrs.cause: The pipe was not properly seated in the former groove, or the bender is the wrong size for the pipe outside diameter.
attrs.fix: Check that the pipe sits in the groove along its full contact length. Confirm the bender is rated for 15 mm pipe.
